question.worked_solution:
First, we find an angle that's coterminal with $-3\pi $ that lies in the range $[0,2\pi ).$

$$
\begin{aligned}-3\pi +2\pi  & =-\pi  \\ -3\pi +2\cdot 2\pi  & =\pi \,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\operatorname{sec}⁡(-3\pi )=\operatorname{sec}⁡\pi .$

The angle $\pi $ is a quadrantal angle. Let's draw out the quadrantal angles on the unit circle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14266176/assets/792a778286533d589a3410223aaf197b07e64ea77566042d7bb8ac13fbad9768.png)

From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\pi $ corresponds to the point $(-1,0).$

Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi =-1.$

Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{sec}⁡\pi =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi }=\frac{1}{-1}=-1.
$$

Therefore, $\operatorname{sec}⁡(-3\pi )=-1.$
